problem.text: A scanning code consists of a $7\times 7$ grid of squares, with some of its squares colored black and the rest colored white. There must be at least one square of each color in this grid of $49$ squares. A scanning code is called symmetric if its look does not change when the entire square is rotated by a multiple of $90^\circ$ counterclockwise around its center, nor when it is reflected across a line joining opposite corners or a line joining midpoints of opposite sides. What is the total number of possible symmetric scanning codes?

steps.title: Where to start: cells that move onto each other must match
steps.body: A symmetric code looks the same after all $8$ moves: the $4$ rotations and the $4$ reflections. If one of these moves carries cell $P$ onto cell $Q$, then $P$ and $Q$ must have the same color. So split the grid into groups of cells that the moves carry onto each other, and count the groups. Careful: use the reflections as well as the rotations.

your_turn.prompt: Put the center cell at $(0,0)$. Which cells are in the same group as the cell $(3,1)$?
your_turn.answer: The $8$ cells $(\pm 3,\pm 1)$ and $(\pm 1,\pm 3)$: rotations and reflections can swap the coordinates and change their signs.

steps.title: Pick one cell from each group
steps.body: Using sign changes and swaps, every cell $(a,b)$ can be moved to exactly one cell with $0\le b\le a\le 3$. That is a thin wedge, roughly one eighth of the grid, and each group has exactly one cell in it. So the number of groups equals the number of cells in the wedge.

your_turn.prompt: How many cells $(a,b)$ satisfy $0\le b\le a\le 3$?

steps.title: Check that the groups fill the grid
steps.body: The center is a group by itself. A cell on the middle row or column, like $(2,0)$, is in a group of $4$. A cell on a diagonal, like $(2,2)$, is also in a group of $4$. Every other cell is in a group of $8$.

your_turn.prompt: How many groups of size $8$ are there, and do all the group sizes add up to $49$?
your_turn.answer: $3$ groups, from $(2,1)$, $(3,1)$ and $(3,2)$. Then $1+3\cdot 4+3\cdot 4+3\cdot 8=49$, so yes.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body: Each of the $10$ groups can be black or white on its own, giving $2^{10}=1024$ symmetric colorings. Two of them, all black and all white, break the rule that both colors appear. So there are $1024-2=1022$ codes. The answer is **(B)**.

wrong_choices.C: $8190=2^{13}-2$ comes from using only the rotations. Rotations alone give $13$ groups, but the reflections join some of them, leaving $10$.
wrong_choices.D: $8192=2^{13}$ comes from using only the rotations and also forgetting to remove the all-black and all-white grids.
